claim: On Tuesday 24 November 2026 the European Parliament adopts its first-reading position on the regulation speeding up environmental assessments (300-day cap) with at least 400 votes in favour.

runs.reason:
**Base rate.** I’d start around 50% for a scheduled vote on a contested EU simplification file to reach 400 votes. The closest comparisons straddle the threshold: Parliament’s sustainability-reporting negotiating position got 382 votes on 13 November 2025, while the narrower “stop-the-clock” measure got 531 on 3 April 2025. That is a small comparison set, not a measured historical rate. ([oeil.europarl.europa.eu](https://oeil.europarl.europa.eu/oeil/en/procedure-document-summary/pdf?id=1861877&utm_source=openai))

**What moves this case.** The Environment Committee’s 4 November vote was a negative signal: the report passed 36–35, with 11 abstentions, and most S&D members voted against. The stronger and newer signal points up: Agence Europe reported on 20 November that EPP, Renew and S&D had jointly tabled a compromise on protected species, and S&D’s 20 November plenary briefing backed that compromise. Parliament’s Legislative Observatory lists the vote for Tuesday, 24 November, which makes an in-window vote likely. ([redmapl3.europarl.europa.eu](https://redmapl3.europarl.europa.eu/RedmapFront/media/reds_iPlRp/A-10-2026-0290/A-10-2026-0290_en.pdf?utm_source=openai))

**Main failure mode.** The text could pass with fewer than 400 votes. The three groups held 401 seats between them at the start of the term, so even with the compromise, absences and defections likely make votes from outside that trio necessary. Some ECR members backed the committee text, but that support may not carry over to the amended proposal. I put about 4% on no qualifying final vote by the deadline, including postponement or referral before that vote, and about 76% on reaching 400 conditional on a qualifying vote taking place. ([results.elections.europa.eu](https://results.elections.europa.eu/en/))

bvious outcome might fail**
Even with the EPP–S&D–Renew compromise deal on Article 8 making adoption of the text at noon on 24 November very likely, reaching the specific threshold of **400 votes in favour** faces tightly balanced arithmetic:
- **Thin margin of the three-party coalition:** EPP (188), S&D (136), and Renew (77) hold exactly 401 seats in total. With a typical Strasbourg Tuesday attendance and voting rate of ~88–90%, those three groups alone only yield around 355 to 365 present voters.
- **Defections and right-wing abstentions:** Environmental NGOs (such as OceanCare on 20 Nov 2026) have campaigned heavily against Article 8 even as amended, meaning 15 to 30 S&D MEPs (such as the Italian or French delegations who led opposition in committee) could still abstain or vote against the final text. Simultaneously, PfE (84 seats) abstained en bloc in committee, and the ECR group (78 seats) was split in committee (5 for, 3 against, 2 abstaining) and noted on 20 November that EPP, Renew, and S&D altered the committee compromise. If S&D suffers moderate defections while the compromise amendments alienate part of ECR and PfE continues to abstain, the final tally of votes in favour could easily land in the 360–395 range.
- **Procedural risk:** Under Rule 60(4), following the vote on the Commission proposal as amended, the rapporteur or a political group could request referral back to committee for interinstitutional negotiations (trilogues). While the criterion counts the vote on the Commission proposal as amended as a decisive vote, any last-minute postponement or referral before that vote represents a small (~3%) tail risk.

Balancing the high likelihood that the EPP–S&D–Renew compromise passes and brings along the bulk of S&D plus ~35–45 pro-simplification ECR MEPs against the real risk that S&D defections and PfE/ECR abstentions keep the "in favour" total just under 400 (between 365 and 399), the probability of reaching at least 400 votes is slightly above even.

EPP, Renew and S&D have already tabled joint compromise amendments on the species-protection provisions that split the committee, expressly so they can be voted on Tuesday.

Base rate: items that reach the final draft agenda with a tabled committee report and plenary amendments are voted on the scheduled day in the large majority of cases (on the order of nine in ten). When EPP, S&D and Renew vote together on a first-reading legislative text in Strasbourg, the yes tally usually clears 400, because those three groups hold about 398 seats and ECR (and parts of other groups) often add further support on simplification files. Related Omnibus VIII votes this autumn landed in the mid-400s to low-600s in favour.

Facts that move this case: the ENVI vote on 4 November was only 36–35–11, with S&D against a right-leaning text. That cuts against an automatic large majority. Offsetting that, the 18–19 November joint amendments (EPP–Renew–S&D) add population-level safeguards, cumulative-impact checks and monitoring while keeping the 300-day cap and the extension of “unintentional” harm. That is the classic pattern for converting a knife-edge committee result into a centrist plenary majority, and Council already has a mandate, so the political incentive is to adopt a position now rather than delay. Strasbourg Tuesday voting participation is typically higher than in Brussels mini-plenaries (often 630–670).

Strongest reason the obvious outcome fails: the three groups alone are only just under 400 seats. If ECR and PfE largely abstain or vote against the safeguarded text, ordinary absences can leave the decisive yes vote in the 350–395 range even though the text is still adopted. A secondary risk is that the crowded Tuesday voting list (several Omnibus and budgetary items in a one-hour slot) pushes this file to Wednesday, which would be outside the window.
